draft_context.source_title: GHS Wireless InfinitePlay isn’t just a marketing name — I’ve used this Glorious gaming headset for weeks and the battery life really is (almost) infinite
draft_context.description: Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay: one-minute review There’s something deeply satisfying about the way Glorious goes about speccing its gaming peripherals. The company has a sharp eye for nonsense, and ruthlessly strips it out of the mice and, now, the headset that it brings to the gaming market. Behold, then, the GHS Wireless InfinitePlay, a wireless gaming headset featuring precisely zero RGB, built around normal-sized 40mm drivers, just quietly getting on with giving you multiplatform audio with infinite battery life and two mic options for $230. With one swappable battery pack placed in the base station, it’s charging ready for use while you have the other one of the pair in your headset. Each one offers 85 hours of use from a full charge, and in case that wasn’t enough, a ‘guardian’ 45mAh built-in battery handles the changeover so you don’t need to turn the headset back on again after you swap. Handy. That same ‘you won’t need it, but just in case…’ ethos is evident in the mic spec. You’ve got a detachable 70Hz-10KHz noise-cancelling mic for when you’re seated, locked in and ready to absolutely bellow at your team-mates away from prying eyes, and a built-in mic to use when you’re out and about using the Bluetooth connection to a mobile device or Nintendo Switch, and don’t fancy looking like an air traffic controller. Yes, it has 2.4GHz and Bluetooth 5.4 connections, swappable with one button press. (Image credit: Future) And that’s a very impressive feature set at any price, but especially for $229.99 / £199.99 / AU$239.99. It’s not even super clear where the concessions have been made to hit the price point. The audio quality is simply good rather than audiophile-grade, but that’s totally in line with what this headset is for: gaming. It’s trying to articulate useful audio cues, not trick your ears into thinking they’re in the expensive seats at an IMAX cinema. Similarly, the construction materials are almost exclusively lightweight, brushed black plastic rather than anything showier, but that serves the sprightly 360g headset weight. One area of that headset build and design I did run into issues with is the headband. Your experience will vary depending on your head size, but I found a degree of pressure that becomes slightly uncomfortable during longer sessions. This being an elasticated suspended band design, it’s possible that this may ease as the band slackens over time, but during the month I’ve been using my unit I do still notice discomfort. Besides that, there’s very little to grumble about. The power button isn’t clearly labelled, and the Bluetooth button can easily be confused for it, but this is a one-time issue. Once you know what’s what, that moment of unintuitive design becomes moot and you can enjoy the fantastic feature set of these cans. Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay: Price and availability List price: $229.99 / £199.99 / AU$239.99 Swappable batteries like the Arctis Nova Pro Wireless, for less Packed with useful extras The extremely competitive pricing of this package is certainly one of its biggest assets. Packing a dual swappable battery design for less than Steelseries’ Arctis Nova Pro Wireless is a great way to announce one’s presence in the headset market, and Glorious backs that head-turning spec up with a number of handy additions that justify the price point. Namely, a choice of mics (detachable or built-in) and a ‘guardian’ built-in battery that kicks in when you swap between the rechargeable packs, along with some serious configuration flexibility offered by the base station and dongle. In this challenging economy, to put it mildly, you’d simply expect to see this package priced higher. The construction materials aren’t comparable with ultra-high-end models like the Audeze Maxwell 2 or the Logitech Astro A50 X , but they’re sturdy and finished to a high standard. Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay: Specs Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay Price $229.99 / £199.99 / AU$239.99 Weight 360g / 0.8lbs Battery life 85 hours per pack Compatibility PC, PS4, PS5, Switch, Android, iPhone Connectivity Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, USB-C wired Microphone 16-bit/48KHz Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay: Design and features Black and orange design is Valve-esque Prioritises light weight over looks Battery packs look like retro FPS keycards There’s a duality here to Glorious’ headset stylings. On the one hand, it's extremely restrained with the brushed black plastic on the base station and headset, an elegant amount of orange contrast trim on the whole package, and battery packs that look like they’d unlock a door in a ‘90’s shooter. On the other hand, the company’s fundamental branding is based on a joke that got old quite a while ago. The brand's name references the glorious PC gaming master race meme and subreddit, which worked as a self-aware joke about PC gaming elitism in 2008 and 2011, but in 2026 works… less so. Look, this could just be an age thing, but to me the GabeN-like brand logo and ‘GGWP’ text on the lower-left earcup feel just a few steps away from a ‘Keep out mom, I’m gaming!’ poster. Given that this headset works with PS5, PS4, Switch and mobile devices (there’s no Xbox version), it’s also just confusing branding at this point. With that chiding out of the way, I do like the look of this headset. The orange trim feels Valve-esque in the right way, like someone very clever sat and thought about this for a long time. The base station is compact and smart, with indicator lights to show when it’s connected to your headset and the charge status of the battery pack slotted into it. Two USB-C ports to the rear connect to a wireless dongle which sits flush with the base station when connected, and a USB-C-to-USB-C cable to connect to your PC or console. A USB-C to A adapter is also provided. (Image credit: Future) The base station, dongle, cables, and Bluetooth connection create tons of setup configurations. You can ditch the base station and just use the dongle if you like, although that does mean you don’t have a spare battery charging while you use it. You can even ditch the dongle too and connect the headset with the USB-C cable, although I haven’t found a use case yet where that makes sense, since the built-in battery has a few hours of life even when both swappable packs are depleted. The headset itself is pretty lightweight for a wireless model with a battery pack, eschewing flashy finishes for an all-plastic body with a fabric headband on suspended elastic, and breathable fabric earcups covering reasonably plush memory foam cushions. If you love that pulsing, sealed-in feeling of closed-back headphones like the HyperX Cloud, these aren’t your cans. They’re certainly closed-back, but the fabric around the earcups does affect the way you experience the audio from its 40mm drivers, producing a flat, detailed but not very low-end heavy response that’s reminiscent of Steelseries’ excellent Arctis Nova 7 and upwards. I don’t get on with the physical control layout here, though. The location of the (unmarked) power button on the upper-left earcup threw me initially, and I think this control and its right-hand earcup mate are trying to do too much. Both are rotary dials as well as buttons, and while the left controls chat mix, profile swapping and battery status, the right controls volume and media controls. I’m all for minimalist design, but try navigating that while you’re concentrating on something in-game. It took me a couple of weeks to memorise how to perform all those actions. Just one more gripe – the battery status readout would be much better if it gave you a percentage rather than simply an ‘ok’ or ‘charge now’. Maybe one for a future firmware update. (Image credit: Future) Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay: Performance Tuned for gaming performance Good suite of software tweaks Battery life true to claims We all know by now that buying a mouse, keyboard, or headset doesn’t turn you into a Faze Clan member, and the gaming performance gains in the headset vertical are especially marginal. That said, if you’re listening out for footsteps in PUBG Battlegrounds and your 2014 cans with their 60mm grotesquely tuned drivers are too busy making a far-off gunfight sound like a drum and bass gig, you might notice a bit of an advantage when you update your audio hardware. That’s why it’s important that these drivers are tuned with a nice flat EQ response. That means that they don’t strongly emphasise one particular area of the EQ spectrum, unlike the aforementioned early 2010s models with their ‘scooped’ profiles that boosted the lows and highs like a sound engineer at a Metallica gig. Sticking with a roughly even volume distribution along the spectrum means that the GHS Wireless InfinitePlay gives all frequencies space to voice and be heard. It might not sound mind-blowing like Audio-Technica or Audeze drivers, but it’s well-suited to games that reward a keen ear, from competitive shooters to singleplayer titles. I find headsets tuned this way really useful in racing sims too, where I need to hear brake lockups and tire squeals as early as possible, and as prominently in the mix as I can. Over in Glorious Core, the accompanying software, there’s a welcome and well-judged suite of options including a sidetone toggle, EQ tuning including some basic provided profiles, mic settings like noise cancellation toggling, and several options to tweak the headset behaviour, like when it auto-powers down and whether it gives you voice prompts. I don’t love that it’s taking up 0.99GB of my SSD space to do that, though, and would much prefer a browser-based tuning app. The battery life really is as long per pack as Glorious states, and swapping them out is easy while you’re mid-session. Just take the spent one out, let the ‘guardian’ battery take over until the end of the round or the next quiet moment, then swap in the other pack. I didn’t run into any setup issues when I used this with PC, PS5 or Switch, and found that the dual-wireless is pretty rock solid. It’s less suited as a console headset, particularly the Switch, since it really needs the base station to be connected in order to keep a battery pack charged and ready. But as a multiplatform solution (marketing types like to call these ‘battle station’ setups), it offers a no-fuss means to switch between devices. (Image credit: Future) Should you buy the Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay? Buy it if... Running out of charge = death This is a hilariously extreme three-battery solution to the age-old wireless dilemma, and it works. You play on a few devices The base station and dongle configuration options make this ideal for multiplatform use. You’ve got a thing for retro shooter keycards These battery packs are unspeakably satisfying to swap in and out. You’ll feel like Doomguy every time. Don't buy it if... You need Xbox compatibility. There’s a long list of devices this headset supports, but Xbox isn’t one of them. If that's what you need, you should look at other models by. Tighter headbands tend to dig in and cause you discomfort There’s some adjustability to this headband, but not loads. If this is a frequent issue, try before you buy. The old PC master race meme makes you cringe When you build your brand on a meme that predates Skyrim , high cringe levels in 2026 are inevitable. Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay: Also consider Not feeling like swapping in this wireless headset? Consider these premium wireless alternatives. Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay Audeze Maxwell 2 Steelseries Arctis Nova Pro Wireless Price $229.99 / £199.99 / AU$239.99 $349.99 / £329.99 / AU$520 $349 (£329, AU$649) Weight 360g / 0.8lbs 490g / 1.1lbs 0.75lbs / 339g Battery life 85 hours 80 hours 36 hours Connection type PC, PS4, PS5, Switch, Android, iPhone 2.4GHz wireless, digital wired (USB-C), analog wired (3.5mm audio jack), Bluetooth Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless Compatibility Bluetooth, 2.4GHz wireless, USB-C wired PC, Xbox (Xbox version only), PS5 (PlayStation version only), Switch, MacOS, iOS, Android Playstation 4/5, PC, Nintendo Switch, iOS, Android Steelseries Arctis Nova Pro Wireless Featuring Steelseries’ unique dual-battery charging solution, premium looks, plus ANC implementation, the Nova Pro Wireless is a premium headset option with few faults. No Xbox version, though, sadly. For more information, check out our full SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Wireless review Audeze Maxwell 2 Goodness, these headphones sound great. The raw audio fidelity out of the box is benchmark-setting and the build quality is audiophile-grade, but Glorious’ model is in the same conversation for a lot less. For more information, check out our full Audeze Maxwell 2 review How I tested the Glorious GHS Wireless InfinitePlay One month of use on PC, PS5, Switch and mobile. All configurations tested Tested with shooters, battle royales, racing games and more Something about the black and orange design of this headset and base station gave me an overwhelming urge to replay Half-Life 2 episodes 1 and 2, so that is where I began. Hearing those familiar audio files through new drivers is a good reference point, actually, which helps to suss out how good the GHS Wireless InfinitePlay is at positional audio. I’ve also been playing PUBG Battlegrounds , Counter-Strike 2 and F1 25 with this headset, and putting the mic through its paces with amateur found footage horror simulator, Content Warning . Since it offers an array of connection types – with or without the base station, wired connection – I’ve spent some time playing on all of them, across my PC, Switch, and PS5. Read more about how we test First reviewed April 2026. ]]>

Tín hiệu từ Thanh Nien Cong Nghe cần được đặt vào bối cảnh trước: thời điểm xuất hiện, chi tiết đã có cơ sở và lý do nó đáng nằm trong dòng tin công nghệ hôm nay. Phần này cần dựng lại thay đổi đã có cơ sở trước khi chuyển sang nhận định.

sections.heading: Tác động thực tế với người đọc
sections.body: Hãng thông tấn Nga TASS cho biết Tổng thống Vladimir Putin đã ký đạo luật đầu tiên, đưa ra quy định toàn diện về việc lưu thông tiền mã hóa và quyền kỹ thuật số tại Nga. Tác động thực tế nằm ở workflow, chi phí, rủi ro hoặc quyết định mua/dùng; Tổng thống Nga Vladimir Putin ký đạo luật lịch sử về tiền mã hóa nên được giải thích qua lăng kính đó trước khi kết luận rộng hơn. Phần này cần nối câu chuyện với workflow, chi phí, bảo mật hoặc quyết định dùng/mua của người đọc.

sections.heading: Chi tiết cần kiểm chứng
sections.body: Luật này đặt ra quy tắc cho các sàn giao dịch tiền mã hóa, bên lưu ký, nhà môi giới, trung tâm/tổ chức thanh toán bù trừ, nhà đầu tư và các bên tham gia thị trường khác. Tuy nhiên, Nga vẫn sẽ duy trì lệnh cấm sử dụng tiền mã hóa làm phương tiện thanh toán hoặc tiền tệ hợp pháp trong nước. Câu hỏi tiếp theo là tín hiệu này có thành rollout bền vững, thay đổi giá trị sản phẩm, giới hạn đáng chú ý hay chỉ là một nhịp cập nhật ngắn. Phần này chỉ giữ chi tiết có thể kiểm chứng và tránh lặp lại nguyên văn cách diễn đạt của nguồn.

sections.heading: Ai nên hành động hoặc chờ
sections.body: Theo luật, các nhà đầu tư cá nhân được phép mua các loại tiền mã hóa có tính thanh khoản cao với mức giới hạn là 300. 000 ruble (3. 700 USD) một năm. Tuy nhiên, báo cáo không nêu rõ loại tài sản tiền mã hóa nào đủ điều kiện. Mặt khác, các nhà đầu tư đủ điều kiện được tự do mua bất kỳ tài sản nào, không bị giới hạn. Với người đọc, khung hữu ích gồm bằng chứng hiện có, nhóm bị ảnh hưởng, rủi ro còn lại và điểm nên kiểm tra trước khi hành động. Phần này cần gọi đúng nhóm độc giả nên hành động ngay hoặc nên chờ thêm xác nhận.

sections.heading: Điều cần theo dõi tiếp
sections.body: Cả hai nhóm này đều phải vượt qua "bài kiểm đặc biệt về mức độ phù hợp". Các nhà đầu tư cá nhân có thể đạt được trạng thái "đủ điều kiện" dựa trên lịch sử giao dịch tiền mã hóa của họ. Một bài tốt cần tách rõ sự kiện từ nguồn, tác động với người đọc và câu hỏi theo dõi để không giống bản tóm tắt link rời. Phần này nên khép lại bằng tín hiệu cần kiểm tra tiếp, không tóm tắt lại cùng một ý.

Chúc bạn đọc báo vui vẻ! --> Tổng thống Vladimir Putin đã ký một đạo luật mang tính bước ngoặt, thiết lập khuôn khổ pháp lý cho thị trường tiền mã hóa tại Nga.
Hãng thông tấn Nga TASS cho biết Tổng thống Vladimir Putin đã ký đạo luật đầu tiên, đưa ra quy định toàn diện về việc lưu thông tiền mã hóa và quyền kỹ thuật số tại Nga.

Luật này đặt ra quy tắc cho các sàn giao dịch tiền mã hóa, bên lưu ký, nhà môi giới, trung tâm/tổ chức thanh toán bù trừ, nhà đầu tư và các bên tham gia thị trường khác. Tuy nhiên, Nga vẫn sẽ duy trì lệnh cấm sử dụng tiền mã hóa làm phương tiện thanh toán hoặc tiền tệ hợp pháp trong nước.

Theo luật, các nhà đầu tư cá nhân được phép mua các loại tiền mã hóa có tính thanh khoản cao với mức giới hạn là 300.000 ruble (3.700 USD) một năm. Tuy nhiên, báo cáo không nêu rõ loại tài sản tiền mã hóa nào đủ điều kiện. Mặt khác, các nhà đầu tư đủ điều kiện được tự do mua bất kỳ tài sản nào, không bị giới hạn.
Cả hai nhóm này đều phải vượt qua "bài kiểm đặc biệt về mức độ phù hợp". Các nhà đầu tư cá nhân có thể đạt được trạng thái "đủ điều kiện" dựa trên lịch sử giao dịch tiền mã hóa của họ.

Trong khi đó, các sàn giao dịch tiền mã hóa được yêu cầu phải tham gia "danh sách đặc biệt" để hoạt động với yêu cầu vốn chủ sở hữu tối thiểu là 15 triệu ruble (185.200 USD). Các sàn giao dịch cũng phải tham gia một tổ chức tự quản lý thị trường tài chính.

draft_context.source_title: The M6 MacBook Pro is coming. Is it worth waiting for?
draft_context.description: Macworld Apple offers the MacBook Pro with three different chip options. It starts with the entry-level M5 chip, which you can only get in the 14-inch MacBook Pro. Apple also offers higher end M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro, as it has since the M1 arrived in 2020. The M5 MacBook Pro was released in October 2025. According to reports, Apple plans to upgrade the laptop to an M6 chip this fall, which isn’t a surprise. What is a surprise is that Apple will reportedly skip the Pro and Max M6 variants to focus on the M7 coming later in 2027. So the M6 MacBook Pro could be the only M6 option available. This article keeps track of the reports about the upcoming M6 MacBook Pro. Keep an eye on this article for the latest news. M6 MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch? • Fall 2026 expected In a July report , Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that the M6 MacBook Pro is expected to ship this fall. Of the five generations of the entry-level MacBook Pro, three have been released in the October/November timeframe, including the past two releases. Here are the release dates for the entry-level MacBook Pro: M5 MacBook Pro : October 2025 M4 MacBook Pro : November 2024 M3 MacBook Pro : January 2023 M2 MacBook Pro : June 2022 M1 MacBook Pro : November 2020 This release could be affected by the memory chip shortage that has been affecting the whole tech industry. If Apple is unable to obtain the quantity of chips it needs, Apple could be forced to move the release date back. Or, there could have a short supply of laptops available, which would result in actual delivery dates slipping. At this point in time, we haven’t heard of any delays. The fall release of the M6 MacBook Pro seems to be on schedule, but the volatility of the chip market could cause it to change unexpectedly. M6 MacBook Pro: Chip details First 2nm M-series chip Redesigned GPU Apple will upgrade the MacBook Pro M5 to an M6 chip, which will be the key upgrade for this release cycle. The chip is expected to be the first M-series chip built using TSMC’s 2nm process . A smaller process allows for more transistors to be placed on the chip, which would result in faster speeds and improved power efficiency. The M6 chip is expected to incorporate new features for improved AI processing. Apple The M5 chip comes with 10 CPU cores: 4 super cores and 6 efficiency cores. No reports have been made about the M6 CPU core count, but Gurman reported that “performance will also improve.” Apple is also planning enhancements for the built-in video codecs. In June, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that the M6 could offer an updated memory architecture and memory bandwidth of 200 GB/s, a 31 percent increase over the M5’s 153 GB/s. Apple will also likely update the chip’s Neural Engine to help AI processing for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. As for the RAM configurations, Apple offers the M5 with 16GB, 24GB, or 32GB of RAM. Apple isn’t expected to change this with the M6. The M6 will also have a redesigned GPU. Gurman reported that Apple tested a version of the M6 with 12 GPU cores, which is two more than the M5. M6 MacBook Pro: Other specifications and features No major changes expected The chip upgrade to the M6 is expected to be the only major change with the back MacBook Pro release. The display, keyboard, trackpad, ports, and other features are all expected to be identical or similar to the M5 MacBook Pro. The M6 MacBook Pro could be the last entry-level model of this particular design. Foundry According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is planning an entry-level M7 MacBook Pro for 2027. This laptop will have a base M7 chip that replaces the M6, but it will also have several new features to match those introduced with the touchscreen MacBook Pro . The entry-level M7 MacBook Pro will have a new design, an OLED display, and other features, but it’s not expected to have a touchscreen. M6 MacBook Pro: Price $1,999 (expected) Ongoing memory constraints could affect configurations We haven’t heard any reports about the price of the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro, but we can look at recent price history to get an idea. When the M5 MacBook Pro was released in 2025, its starting price was $1,599. Apple bumped it to $1,699 when the M5 Pro and Max models arrived earlier this year and increased the starting storage to 1TB. This past June, however, Apple raised the price to $1,999 due to supply chain constraints. Those constraints aren’t going away anytime soon, and it’s likely that the higher price is now the new normal . During Apple’s Q3 2026 financial announcement in July, Apple CEO Tim Cook and CFO Kevan Parekh made it a point to explain that the supply chain constraints will affect production costs for months to come. ” We expect the impact from supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially,” said Parekh. “The projected supply constraints in the September quarter affect iPhone, Mac, and iPad.” Cook said, “With less flexibility in supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially.” With this in mind, it’s quite possible that prices could go up again with the release of the M6 MacBook Pro. It’s unlikely, but the state of the chip supply chain will influence what prices Apple will offer. Considering that the M7 MacBook Pro won’t be far from replacing the yet-to-be-released M6 MacBook Pro, one strategy Apple could employ is to price the M6 MacBook Pro at the same $1,999 price and push any price hikes to the next generation. If that’s the case, the M6 could be a good option for anyone on the fence about upgrading.

draft_context.description: Macworld At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Affordable for four bays Dual 5Gbe connections Tons of apps and capabilities Excellent performance Unlimited IP cams in surveillance app Cons Drive trays don’t lock Requires mail address during initialization TOS 7 still slightly buggy Our Verdict TerraMaster’s F4-425 is a fast, versatile, four-bay storage, backup and media streaming NAS box that’s every bit as good as, if not better than similar units from QNAP and Synology. Especially as the company doesn’t gouge you for IP cam licenses. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed $639 Best Prices Today: TerraMaster F4-425 Pro Retailer Price $699.99 View Deal TerraMaster $800 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Product Price Price comparison from Backmarket I’m always surprised how few people own a NAS (Network Attached Storage) box such as the highly capable F4-425 Pro reviewed here. NAS requires a bit more tech savvy than cloud services and storage, plus some upfront cost, but there’s one particular reason it’s worth it: complete and private control of the apps, services, and most importantly –the data you store on it. Internet outage? Doesn’t affect your NAS. Online data breech? Doesn’t affect your NAS. Monthly payments? Only to your power company. Simply put, NAS is fantastic for data backup and streaming media about the house and can also serve as the engine for a home surveillance network. We like NAS, and TerraMaster has quickly become one of our favorite consumer flavors thanks to excellent hardware and apps, a newly faster OS, and the lack of surcharges vendors such as QNAP and Synology hit you up with for things such as additional IP cam licenses. That said, there was the occasional immaturity in the apps and operating system. What are the F4-425 Pro’s features? The F4-425 Pro is a silver and black hued, mostly metal, four-bay NAS box with quick swap, non-locking 3.5-inch drive trays. It measures approximately 7.1-inches wide by 8.6-inches deep, by 5.9-inches tall and weighs around 6.5 pounds bare. That will of course increase as you add drives. If you remove the four screws on the bottom holding the aluminum body to the chassis, you’ll find three PCIe 3.0 NVMe M.2 slots that accept NVMe SSDs. There’s enough space for heat sinks, which would be a good idea to prolong SSD life. Note that you can use PCIe 4.0/5.0 SSDs but they’ll be limited to PCIe 3.0 speed. The front of the unit provides access to the four drive bays, as well as the power button and a single 10Gbps USB Type-A port. The back is home to an additional pair of 10Gbps Type-A USB ports, twin 5Gbe Ethernet ports, and HDMI port (console use only), and a single Type-C port for diagnostics and the like. There’s also the power jack, a pinhole reset button, and a rather massive exhaust fan. The back of the F4-425 Pro with its dual 2.5Gbpe and 10GBps Type-A ports. There’s a Type-C port but it’s only for diagnostics. The HDMI port is for console (command prompt) use only. The processor inside of our test unit was a capable 8-core Intel N350 with a substantial 16GB of DDR5 onboard. That’s plenty of power for advanced tasks like virtual machines and Docker. TerraMaster also provides several apps for backup up mobile devices, and even controlling the box. The TNAS mobile app on install and first use. TerraMaster provides 2-year warranty on the F4-425 Pro. And thankfully, the company now also provides a downloadable PDF user’s guide. How is the F4-425 Pro’s setup? Adding drives to the tool-less trays is largely painless: slide them out, pop out the side rails, slip in the 3.5-inch HDD and replace the side rails. Screws are provided for 2.5-inch hard drives or SATA SSDs. As described above, you’ll need to remove the outer shell to access the three PCIe 3.0 NVMe slots. lWhen you first boot the F4-425 (and most TerraMaster NAS) it presents a dialog asking for your email address to receive a code. That’s of course after you find its IP address (E.g. 192/168.1.110) and visit with your browser. Below the email field, in very light lettering, is the ability to bypass this step. If you choose, you can activate your online presence with TerraMaster during setup. Alas, you still have to enter your email. I don’t like sending info to a company until I’m very familiar with the hardware and said company. I wish TerraMaster would abandon this practice ad to be blunt–it’s none of their darn business. To be fair, you can put the F4-425 Pro into “Security Isolation Mode” (Control Panel / Security/ Security Isolation Mode) after setup, to prevent any further traffic outside of your local network. The F4-425 also features a highly configurable firewall if that’s too drastic a measure for you. What is the F4-425 Pro’s operating system and software like? The F4-425 Pro delivered our first look at the latest version 7 of TOS (TerraMaster Operating System), a substantially feature-equivalent but far better-performing version of the operating system (version 6) than I tested with the F2-425 . Especially in regards multitasking. Beyond that, it appeared to me to be more evolutionary than revolutionary, despite heralding itself as the first AI-enabled NAS OS. It does allow you to install OpenCLAW which enables normal language access to various features. TerraMaster says OpenCLAW makes things easier, but the real issue with most new NAS users is that they don’t know what to ask, let alone how to ask it. Actually, thinking about it, that’s the issue with just about any AI system. Note also that the minute I opened OpenCLAW, the F4-425 Pro’s fan kicked into high gear. It takes some juice. That said, I quite like TOS, it’s as well laid out as the QNAP and Synology equivalents, and perhaps a bit more intuitive. However, I found version 7 a bit buggy. Rough around the edges, as it were. I stuck with TOS 7 as it’s so much quicker at everything than version 6 but there were some annoyances such as the inability to include spaces in a backup job name, and not automatically resuming jobs that were not completed in the last session. I’d also be careful doing searches and deleting the results with the file manager. There are also tons of apps for backup, surveillance, development, and multimedia streaming. Below is my favorite: Centralized Backup, which can back up from numerous sources (SMB, FTP, etc.) without the need to install clients on every machine. Simply share the folders or files you want across the network, locate them and create a job to back them up. I love Centralized Backup’s ability to back up my shared folders without me having to install client software on the involved computers. Centralized Backup, along with CloudSync (back up to a host of online services) are my favorite TOS backup apps, but there are quite a few others (Duple Vault, Elephant Drive, etc.) as well as TerraMaster’s own client-based, portal driven TerraSync. There’s also a handy folder mirroring utility (TFM) that you can use across volumes. eAll the backup and sync options offered by TOS 7. Want to keep tabs on your house? TerraMaster includes Surveillance Manager (shown below), which offers support for unlimited cameras. This is in distinct contrast to Synology and QNAP which limit you to one or two cameras so they can sell you more licenses. This is one of the best reasons to opt for a TerraMaster NAS box, however, note that you’ll have to configure your router to reach the app remotely. The Surveillance Manager opens in a separate tab and allows up to tk IP cams. While I use TOS’s DLNA Multimedia Server to stream movies to my TV, TerraMaster also includes the extremely popular Plex (shown below), as well as Jellyfin and Emby for fans of those systems. The extremely popular Plex Media Server is present in TOS 7. TRAID is TerraMaster’s hybrid RAID solution (all NAS vendors have one these days) that combines mirroring (RAID 1) and parity (RAID 5). It allows you to combine drives of different sizes while using more of their capacity than standard RAID modes do. Generally speaking, most RAID modes allow you to use only the capacity of each drive in the array equal to that of the smallest drive in the array. Combine a 4TB HDD and an 8TB HDD in RAID 0 (striping) or RAID 1 (mirroring), and only 4TB of the 8TB drive is used, while the rest just sits there. TRAID and similar solutions let you employ the otherwise wasted capacity as another volume, or part of one. How much is the F4-425? The F4-425 Pro with the Intel N350 retails for $799, but was on sale at TerraMaster’s site for $639 at the time of this writing. From TerraMaster’s Amazon store make that $699. There’s a cheaper $569 Intel N305/8GB version of the F4-425 Pro available, as well as less endowed $599 F4-425 Plus (Intel N150 processor, 16GB), and $429 F4-425 (quad-core, 4GB) models if the Pro is too pricey for you, or you don’t need to run VMs, Docker, etc. The Plus and plain versions were discounted to $480 and $344 respectively at the time of this writing. All use the same operating system and offer the same applications. The F4-425 Pro’s price is roughly on par for a NAS box with this grade of processor, 16GB of memory and NVMe slots, but as always — shop around, though we’re fairly sure you’d be happiest with the TerraMaster. How does the F4-425 perform? The F4-425 Pro features dual 5Gbpe (Multi-gig) so it’s capable of nearly 600MBps when using that protocol, and around 1GBps if you aggregate the two 5Gbps Ethernet adapters. At 2.5Gbps, expect around 290MBps, and on gigabit, around 140Mbps. There’s no Wi-Fi, but that’s not the best way to use a NAS box. You can with some (and an add-in card), but commonly NAS is connected via Ethernet directly to a router or switch. I populated the F4-425 with a single 1.92GB Seagate IronWolf SATA SSD and two Crucial T710 PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSDs (running at PCIe 3.0 speed) and formatted with the Btrfs file system. All those SSDs are massively faster than 5Gbpe or even 10Gbpe. The test network consisted of my M4 Max Studio, an EnGenius ECS2512FP 12-port switch (8 x 2.5Gbe/4 x 10Gbe), and PCWorld’s 10Gbe Intel testbed. I tested with both a single 5Gbe Ethernet connection and both 5Gbe Ethernet ports bonded using TOS 7. However, there was so little improvement with the ports bonded, I’m showing only the 5Gbe results. As to that… Disk Speed Test was quite complimentary of the F4-425’s throughput, and more so than AmorphousDiskMark. Disk Speed Test was complimentary of the F4-425’s throughput, and more so than AmorphousDiskMark. AmorphousDiskMark writes more data at a time than Disk Speed Test, which may be the reason for the lower write number. That said, CrystalDiskMark on the PC showed even greater performance that Disk Speed Test — 587MBps reading and 580GBps writing. AmorphousDiskMark writes more data at a time than Disk Speed Test, which may be the reason for the lower write number. That said, CrystalDiskMark on the PC showed even greater performance that Disk Speed Test — 587MBps reading and 470GBps writing. ATTO was more in line with Disk Speed Test than AmorphousDiskMark. ATTO was more in line with Disk Speed Test than AmorphousDiskMark. As to sprightlyness, I banged on the interface and apps pretty hard. The F4-425 Pro was extremely responsive. Tasks completely quickly, including firmware updates and reboots. The latter were far faster than what I’m used to with my older NAS boxes. Multi-tasking, which I complained about with TOS 6 on the F2-425 was light years better. Thank you TOS 7! And of course, more memory and a faster processor. TerraMaster’s advertising teases over 1GBps performance. However, that’s simply totaling two separate 500GBps connections working separately. Expect what you see above. Note also that there is a list of compatible NVMe SSDs found here . I’ve had issues with the F8 SSD Plus with some that weren’t supported, though the F4-425 seems fine with the same SSDs. I also found that some software required re-enabling after reboots or shutdowns in TOS 7. Should I buy the F4-425 Pro? If you need a very fast 4-Bay NAS box, the TerraMaster F4-425 fits the bill. Though you should expect a couple of software glitches here and there with TOS 7 that QNAP and Synology don’t suffer. That said, for creating a surveillance system, the lack of additional fees makes it top dog in that department.
paragraphs: TerraMaster’s F4-425 is a fast, versatile, four-bay storage, backup and media streaming NAS box that’s every bit as good as, if not better than similar units from QNAP and Synology. Especially as the company doesn’t gouge you for IP cam licenses.

I’m always surprised how few people own a NAS (Network Attached Storage) box such as the highly capable F4-425 Pro reviewed here. NAS requires a bit more tech savvy than cloud services and storage, plus some upfront cost, but there’s one particular reason it’s worth it: complete and private control of the apps, services, and most importantly –the data you store on it.

Internet outage? Doesn’t affect your NAS. Online data breech? Doesn’t affect your NAS. Monthly payments? Only to your power company. Simply put, NAS is fantastic for data backup and streaming media about the house and can also serve as the engine for a home surveillance network.

We like NAS, and TerraMaster has quickly become one of our favorite consumer flavors thanks to excellent hardware and apps, a newly faster OS, and the lack of surcharges vendors such as QNAP and Synology hit you up with for things such as additional IP cam licenses.

The F4-425 Pro is a silver and black hued, mostly metal, four-bay NAS box with quick swap, non-locking 3.5-inch drive trays. It measures approximately 7.1-inches wide by 8.6-inches deep, by 5.9-inches tall and weighs around 6.5 pounds bare. That will of course increase as you add drives.
